title: The best gift (351–359)
hook: the gift of the dhamma beats all gifts; its taste beats all tastes (Dhammapada 354)

segments.voice: Yesterday, jāla, the web: craving spins its own, and what you spun, you can step out of. Today, the end of the chapter on thirst.

Some of the gifts that last aren't things at all. They're sentences someone said at the right moment. A teacher who told you that you were good at something. A grandparent who showed you how to do a thing with your hands. A friend who said, you don't have to carry this alone. The object wears out; the sentence doesn't. The commentary says today's verse answered a question the gods themselves were arguing about.
screen: `GIFTS THAT AREN'T THINGS.` → `OFTEN IT'S A SENTENCE.` → `A QUESTION THE GODS ARGUED.`

segments.voice: In the heaven of the thirty-three gods, the commentary says, the devas got into a debate. Which gift is best? Which taste is best? Which delight is best? No one could settle it, so Sakka, their king, came down to ask the Buddha. The answer is verse three hundred fifty-four, in Max Müller's English: "The gift of the law exceeds all gifts; the sweetness of the law exceeds all sweetness; the delight in the law exceeds all delights; the extinction of thirst overcomes all pain." Where Müller says the law, the Pali says dhamma: the teaching, the way things truly are. So the best gift is the teaching. Buddhist tradition calls it dhamma-dana, the gift of dhamma, and says it outshines even gifts of food and robes, which are themselves honored. The last line ties the whole chapter together: the end of thirst, of tanha, ends all pain. The creeper, the root, the web all come undone. The chapter's other verses circle the same place. Tradition places one soon after his awakening, as the Buddha's reply when a wandering ascetic asked who his teacher was: I have conquered all, I know all, and I have no teacher. Another says riches ruin the foolish, but not those who seek the far shore. And the chapter closes with fields: fields are spoiled by weeds, and people are spoiled by passion, hatred, delusion and lust. Gifts given to those free of these weeds, the verses say, bring great reward. The verse doesn't keep the gift of the dhamma for monks. One true teaching, passed on at the right moment, is a small share of it.
screen: `SAKKA'S QUESTION.` · `THE GIFT OF THE DHAMMA EXCEEDS ALL.` · `THE END OF THIRST ENDS ALL PAIN.` · `FIELDS SPOILED BY WEEDS.` · then, large: `THE BEST GIFT.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last few weeks of verses, the forest, the bigger joy, the elephant bearing the arrow, the creeper, the web, and pick one line that has stayed with you. Think of one person who might need that line right now, and hold the two together, the verse and the person, wishing them well. Then rest with the breath.
Dhammadāna. The gift of the dhamma, the teaching: it exceeds all gifts, and the end of thirst ends all pain.
Your line: fields are spoiled by weeds. The gift of the dhamma exceeds all gifts. Day two hundred twenty-one, done.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists sponsor the printing of dhamma books to give away, and teachers describe the gift of the dhamma (dhamma-dana) as the highest gift; lay people often dedicate the merit of giving to others.

original.note: Pali dhammadāna: the gift of the dhamma; verse 354 calls it the gift that exceeds all gifts.

trapdoor: what you thought: the best gift is the most expensive one.
what it means: the gift of the dhamma, the teaching, exceeds all gifts; the end of thirst ends all pain.
what a scholar hears: 'sabbadanam dhammadanam jinati': the commentary sets it as the answer to Sakka's four questions, and verse 353 is the Buddha's reply to the ascetic Upaka.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)

notes: Review 2026-10-01: hook rewritten (it opened 'Think of the best gift', and claimed what 'a lot of people' feel); verses 356–359 now name the text's four weeds, not three, and 'the greatest fruit' corrected to Müller's 'great reward'; closing line no longer asserts what counts as the gift.
Müller's verse 354 verified exact against Gutenberg #2017.
Commentary: Sakka and the Tavatimsa devas debate four questions; confirm.
Verse 353 is traditionally the Buddha's reply to the Ajivika Upaka on the road to Benares (MN 26 / Vinaya Mahavagga 1); paraphrased as 'I have conquered all, I know all, I have no teacher'.
Verses 356–359: Müller's four weeds are passion, hatred, vanity (moha, rendered 'delusion' here) and lust; the teach and match now name all four (the draft named three).
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
